stories.title: The JFK *Assassination*
stories.hook: President John F. Kennedy was shot dead in Dallas in 1963. Two days later, the man accused of killing him was shot dead on live television. America has been arguing ever since.
stories.verdictNote: Every official inquiry found that Oswald fired the fatal shots. A 1979 committee called a conspiracy "probable", but its key evidence was later discredited. No conspiracy has been proven.

story: At 12:30 pm on Friday 22 November 1963, President John F. Kennedy's open-top limousine turned into Dealey Plaza in Dallas, Texas. Crowds had cheered him all the way. Moments earlier, Nellie Connally, the Texas governor's wife, had turned round to tell him that no one could say Dallas didn't love him. Then shots rang out. Kennedy was hit in the neck and head; Governor John Connally, sitting in front of him, was badly wounded. Thirty minutes later, at Parkland Hospital, the President was pronounced dead.

Within hours police arrested **Lee Harvey Oswald**, a 24-year-old former Marine who worked in the Texas School Book Depository overlooking the route, and who had shot and killed a police officer, J. D. Tippit, less than an hour after the assassination. Oswald denied killing anyone. Two days later, as he was being moved through the basement of Dallas police headquarters, nightclub owner **Jack Ruby** stepped out of the crowd and shot him dead, on live television.

With the accused assassin gone before any trial, many questions would never be tested in court. In 1964 the Warren Commission concluded that Oswald acted alone, firing three shots from a sixth-floor window, and found no evidence that Oswald or Ruby were part of a conspiracy. Its "single-bullet theory", that one bullet passed through Kennedy and went on to wound Connally, became one of the most argued-over details of the case.

Doubt grew anyway. In 1979 the House Select Committee on Assassinations agreed that Oswald fired the shots that killed Kennedy, but said there was "probably" a conspiracy, mainly because of an acoustic analysis of a police radio recording that seemed to show a fourth shot. That analysis was later discredited. Gallup polls since 1963 have consistently found that at least half, and usually most, Americans doubt that Oswald acted alone.

The theories point at the Mafia, the CIA, Cuba, the Soviet Union and more. Millions of pages of government files have now been released, with a final batch of more than 60,000 documents in March 2025. They revealed plenty of embarrassing secrets but no proof of a plot. What remains is a real tragedy, a strange and troubled accused assassin, and a national wound that never quite healed.

known: Kennedy was shot at 12:30 pm on 22 November 1963 in Dealey Plaza, Dallas, and pronounced dead at 1:00 pm. Governor John Connally was wounded but survived.
Lee Harvey Oswald worked in the Texas School Book Depository overlooking the route. He was arrested about 70 minutes later, after shooting police officer J. D. Tippit.

known.text: A rifle found on the sixth floor had been bought by mail order under one of Oswald's aliases, "A. Hidell".

known: Jack Ruby killed Oswald on live TV two days later. Ruby's conviction was overturned on appeal and he died in prison in 1967, awaiting a new trial.

The Warren Commission (1964) found that Oswald acted alone. The House Select Committee (1979) agreed that he fired the fatal shots but suggested a probable conspiracy, based mainly on acoustic evidence that was later discredited.
Most of the US government's assassination records have been released, with the last large batch in 2025.
speculation: **A second gunman on the "grassy knoll".** Some witnesses thought shots came from a small hill in front of the motorcade. No gunman, weapon or bullet from there has ever been found, and the acoustic "fourth shot" was discredited.
**The CIA did it.** The CIA really did hide things, including plots to kill Fidel Castro and what it knew about Oswald, which fuels suspicion. No evidence shows it planned the killing.
**The Mafia did it.** Organised-crime bosses had motives, and Ruby knew mob figures. The 1979 committee thought mobsters might have been involved, but nothing has been proven.
**Cuba or the Soviet Union.** Oswald had lived in the USSR and visited the Soviet and Cuban embassies in Mexico City weeks earlier. Investigations found no evidence either government was behind it.

speculation.text: **The "magic bullet" is impossible.** Critics say one bullet couldn't wound both men and stay nearly intact, and three of the Warren Commission's own members found it improbable. But a 1964 reenactment found the path consistent with both men's wounds, and a House committee pathologist noted the bullet was in fact deformed. The debate continues.

whyPeopleWonder: It feels wrong that one unhappy, unremarkable man could change history with a cheap mail-order rifle. Psychologists call this **proportionality bias**: we expect huge events to have huge causes, so "a lone gunman" feels like an answer that's too small.

The story also ends in the worst way for the truth. Oswald was killed before a trial could test the evidence, by a man with shady connections. Then, in the 1970s, investigations revealed that the CIA and FBI really had hidden things. Once you know some secrets were kept, it's easy to believe all of them were.

Finally, it was the first great tragedy of the television age. Millions watched the aftermath, and Oswald's murder, live. The Zapruder film has been studied frame by frame for 60 years, and when you look that hard at anything, you'll find something that seems odd.

funFact.text: The mysterious "Umbrella Man", who opened a black umbrella on a sunny day just as the shots rang out, came forward in 1978. Louie Steven Witt told Congress he was heckling Kennedy with a symbol of his father's support for appeasing Hitler. He said that if there were a record for doing the wrong thing at the wrong time in the wrong place, he would be number one.

stories.depthNote: Bottomless. Thousands of books, millions of pages of files, and 60 years of argument over every frame of film.

stories.title: The Moon Landing *Hoax*
stories.hook: Twelve astronauts, 382 kg of Moon rock and a flag that seems to wave. Did NASA really fake it in a studio?
stories.verdictNote: The landings are among the best-documented events of the 20th century, tracked even by America's Cold War rival.

story: On 20 July 1969, around 600 million people watched grainy pictures of Neil Armstrong stepping onto the Moon. A few years later, a surprising idea began to spread: what if they had watched a TV show? What if the whole thing had been filmed on a set somewhere in the Nevada desert?

The theory took off in 1976, when Bill Kaysing, a former technical writer at the rocket-engine maker Rocketdyne, self-published a book called *We Never Went to the Moon*. His arguments became the classics: there are no stars in the photos, the flag seems to wave in a place with no wind, the shadows point in odd directions, and the Van Allen radiation belts should have killed anyone who flew through them.

The idea got a huge boost in 2001, when the Fox network aired a prime-time special asking *Did We Land on the Moon?* A 1999 Gallup poll found that about 6% of Americans doubted the landings happened, but online it has never really gone away.

Here's the thing: every one of those clues has a down-to-earth answer, and the evidence for the landings is enormous. Twelve astronauts walked on the Moon across six missions. They brought back **382 kg of rock and soil** that scientists all over the world have studied for decades. They left mirrors on the surface that observatories still bounce lasers off today. And the Soviet Union, which was racing America to the Moon and would have loved to expose a fake, tracked the missions and never cried foul.

Since 2009, NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter has photographed the landing sites from orbit. You can see the leftover descent stages, the experiments, and even the trails of footprints and rover tracks, still sitting there in the dust.

known: Twelve astronauts walked on the Moon during six landings between July 1969 and December 1972.

Apollo crews brought back 382 kg (842 lb) of lunar rock and soil, studied by scientists around the world. The samples formed without water and are peppered with tiny micrometeorite craters, which is very hard to fake.
Apollo 11, 14 and 15 left mirrors (retroreflectors) on the surface. Observatories still fire lasers at them to measure the Earth–Moon distance.
The Soviet Union, America's rival in the space race, tracked the missions and never claimed they were faked.
NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter has photographed the landing sites, showing hardware, tracks and footpaths.
The flag looked like it was waving because it had a horizontal rod along the top and stayed wrinkled from being packed. It moved only when the astronauts twisted the pole.
speculation: **"There are no stars."** The cameras were set for the dazzling, sunlit surface, so faint stars didn't show up. Photos of a floodlit stadium at night don't show stars either.
**"The flag is waving."** It only moves while astronauts handle it. With no air to slow it down, it actually keeps swinging longer than it would on Earth.
**"The shadows aren't parallel, so there were studio lights."** Bumpy ground and wide-angle lenses make shadows from a single light source look like they point in different directions.

**"The radiation belts would have killed them."** Apollo passed through the Van Allen belts quickly, on paths that avoided the most intense parts. The astronauts wore dosimeters, and their measured doses were modest.

**"Stanley Kubrick filmed it."** A popular joke that became a rumour. There's no evidence, and dust kicked up by the lunar rover flies in clean arcs and falls straight back down, which only happens in a vacuum.
whyPeopleWonder: The hoax theory was born in the mid-1970s, right after the Vietnam War and the Watergate scandal had shown Americans that their government could lie to them about big things. Once trust is broken, a story as huge as "we flew people to the Moon" can start to feel too good to be true.

There's also an odd technology puzzle: the Apollo guidance computer was far weaker than a modern phone, and no one has been back since 1972. Both facts have dull explanations (careful engineering, and politics and money), but they *feel* suspicious.

Finally, Apollo produced thousands of photos and hours of film. If you look hard enough at that much material, you will always find something that looks strange. Psychologists call this **anomaly hunting**: collecting oddities while ignoring the mountain of evidence around them.

funFact.text: Buzz Aldrin saw the Apollo 11 flag blown over by the exhaust as the lunar module blasted off. Photos taken from lunar orbit in 2012 show that the flags from Apollo 12, 16 and 17 are still standing: you can see their shadows.

stories.depthNote: Thousands of photos to argue over and decades of debate, but every claim has been answered in detail.

stories.title: 9/11 *Theories*
stories.hook: Within a few years of the deadliest terrorist attack in history, a question spread online: what if it wasn't what it seemed? Engineers, investigators and journalists checked every claim.
stories.verdictNote: The attacks were carried out by 19 al-Qaeda hijackers. Investigations found serious intelligence failures, not a plot by the US government.

story: On the morning of 11 September 2001, 19 hijackers from the terrorist network **al-Qaeda** took control of four passenger jets. Two were flown into the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center in New York and one into the Pentagon, near Washington, D.C. The fourth crashed in a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, after its passengers and crew fought back. The attacks killed 2,977 people, the deadliest terrorist attack in history.

It was one of the most filmed and most investigated days ever. Even so, within a few years alternative explanations were spreading fast, especially through a 2005 online film called *Loose Change*. Some said the towers were brought down by explosives planted inside, or that a missile, not a plane, hit the Pentagon. Others claimed the US government knew in advance and let it happen, or even made it happen.

Many theories focus on a third building, **7 World Trade Center**, a 47-storey tower that collapsed late that afternoon without being hit by a plane. To many viewers, videos of its fall look like a controlled demolition.

Engineers studied all of it. The US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) concluded that the Twin Towers fell because the impacts stripped fireproofing from the steel and the fires then weakened it. 7 WTC, hit by debris from the North Tower, burned uncontrolled for nearly seven hours. NIST found that heat made steel beams expand until a key column failed, starting a collapse. Magazines including *Popular Mechanics* and *Scientific American* checked the most popular claims one by one and found that they didn't hold up.

What investigators *did* find was real and troubling. The 9/11 Commission documented serious failures by US intelligence agencies, which had warning signs they didn't connect. Failing to stop a plot is very different from organising one, but for some people the first fed suspicion of the second.

known: Nineteen al-Qaeda hijackers seized four planes on 11 September 2001. The attacks killed 2,977 people.
The passengers and crew of Flight 93 learned of the earlier attacks by phone and revolted; the plane crashed near Shanksville.
NIST found that the Twin Towers collapsed after plane impacts stripped fireproofing and fires weakened the steel structure.
NIST found that 7 WTC collapsed because of uncontrolled fires that caused thermal expansion and the failure of a key column. It found no evidence of explosives.
The 9/11 Commission documented serious failures in sharing and acting on intelligence before the attacks.

known.text: Osama bin Laden at first denied involvement, then took responsibility for the attacks in a 2004 video.

speculation: **Controlled demolition of the towers.** No evidence of explosives was found, and preparing a skyscraper for demolition takes weeks of very visible work. Claims of thermite in the dust have been challenged by other scientists.

speculation.text: **"Jet fuel can't melt steel beams."** True, but it doesn't need to. Steel loses about half its strength at around 600 °C, far below its melting point, which is enough to bring a loaded structure down.

speculation: **A missile hit the Pentagon.** Witnesses saw the plane, wreckage was recovered, and the remains of the passengers were identified.
**Flight 93 was shot down, or landed safely somewhere.** The cockpit voice recorder captured the passengers' revolt, and the wreckage was at Shanksville.
**The government let it happen.** The Commission found missed warnings, poor communication and bureaucratic failure, not a deliberate decision to stand aside.
whyPeopleWonder: When something this terrible happens, the official explanation, a small group of men with box cutters exploiting gaps in security, can feel unbearably small. A secret plot by powerful people at least means someone was in control.

Trust also took a hit in the years that followed. The 2003 invasion of Iraq was justified partly by claims about weapons of mass destruction that turned out to be wrong. For many people, that made it easier to believe that the government might lie about 9/11 too.

And 9/11 theories grew up with online video. Films like *Loose Change* could reach millions without any fact-checking, and clips of 7 WTC's collapse, seen without context, are genuinely striking. Understanding why it fell takes engineering reports, not a 30-second clip.

funFact.text: The 9/11 Commission's final report, a government document, became a surprise bestseller and was a finalist for the National Book Award in 2004, praised for reading like a thriller.

stories.title: Area 51 & *Roswell*
stories.hook: In 1947 the US Army announced it had captured a flying saucer. The next day it said: never mind, it's a weather balloon. Neither statement was the whole truth.
stories.verdictNote: The secret base is real, and so was a cover story. The aliens are the part with no evidence.

story: In the summer of 1947, a rancher named Mac Brazel found a field of strange debris near Corona, New Mexico: strips of rubber, shiny foil, tough paper and thin wooden sticks. He reported it to the sheriff, who called the nearby Roswell Army Air Field. On 8 July, the base did something astonishing. It issued a press release saying it had recovered a **"flying disc"**.
Within hours, a general in Texas corrected the story: it was a weather balloon. Reporters were shown the torn foil and sticks, newspapers moved on, and Roswell was mostly forgotten for thirty years.

Then, in 1978, a retired officer who had handled the debris, Jesse Marcel, said in interviews that he believed it was not of this Earth. Books and TV shows followed, and the story grew with each telling: a crashed saucer, alien bodies, a military cover-up. Many of the witness accounts surfaced decades after the event.

Meanwhile, in the Nevada desert, there really was a secret base. Area 51, at Groom Lake, was set up by the CIA in 1955 to test the U-2 spy plane, and later other secret aircraft. For decades the government wouldn't talk about it: the Air Force only acknowledged the site in the 1990s, and the CIA published its own history of the base in 2013. Planes that flew higher and faster than anything the public knew about, from a base that officially wasn't there? It was a perfect home for alien rumours.

So what crashed at Roswell? In the 1990s the US Air Force published reports explaining it as **Project Mogul**, a top-secret program that flew long chains of balloons carrying microphones to listen for Soviet nuclear tests. The "weather balloon" was a cover story for a real secret. A 2024 Pentagon report also found no evidence that the US government has ever recovered alien technology.

known: Something did crash on a New Mexico ranch in 1947, and the Army first called it a "flying disc" before saying it was a weather balloon.
The weather-balloon explanation was itself a cover story. The debris came from Project Mogul, a classified program to detect Soviet nuclear tests with high-flying balloon trains.
Area 51 is a real, highly secret Air Force facility that has tested spy planes like the U-2 and the A-12, and later stealth aircraft.

known.text: The secret U-2 spy plane, tested at Area 51 from 1955, caused a rise in UFO reports in the 1950s: airline pilots saw its silver wings catch the setting sun far above them.

known: The 1995 "alien autopsy" film turned out to be staged. Its producer admitted in 2006 that it was a "reconstruction".
Multiple official reviews (US Air Force 1994 and 1997, Pentagon 2024) found no evidence of alien craft or bodies.
speculation: **A saucer crashed and alien bodies were recovered.** Rests mainly on testimony gathered 30–50 years later. No physical evidence has ever surfaced.

speculation.text: **Alien craft are reverse-engineered at Area 51.** Bob Lazar's story is famous, but the universities he said he attended have no record of him.

speculation: **There's an ongoing cover-up.** In 2023 a former intelligence official told Congress he'd heard of secret recovery programs. He offered no direct evidence, and the Pentagon's 2024 review found none.
**The base is still hiding secrets.** Almost certainly true. But aircraft programmes and military testing are ordinary secrets, not aliens.
whyPeopleWonder: This is the rare conspiracy theory with a **real cover-up inside it**. The government did put out a misleading story about Roswell, and it did hide a base in the Nevada desert for decades. Once you know that, it's natural to ask what else they were hiding.

Stories with a kernel of truth are the most durable kind. Add a Cold War full of secret weapons, unexplained lights in the sky, and blockbusters like *Close Encounters*, *Independence Day* and *The X-Files*, and Roswell became a modern legend.
Today the town of Roswell embraces it, with a UFO museum and an annual UFO festival. The mystery is also good for business.

funFact.text: In 1996 Nevada officially named State Route 375, the lonely road nearest Area 51, the **Extraterrestrial Highway**. The tiny town of Rachel, near its midpoint, caters to UFO-seeking tourists with alien-themed businesses.

stories.depthNote: Decades of books, declassified documents, government reports and a whole town built around the legend.

stories.title: The *Illuminati*
stories.hook: A secret society that secretly runs the world, leaving clues on dollar bills and in music videos. It was real, briefly: for about nine years, in Bavaria, in the 1700s.
stories.verdictNote: The Bavarian Illuminati existed from 1776 until it was crushed in the 1780s. There's no evidence it survived, let alone took over the world.

story: On 1 May 1776, a young law professor named Adam Weishaupt met four of his students in Ingolstadt, Bavaria, and founded a secret society. Its symbol was the owl of Minerva, the Roman goddess of wisdom. Members used code names; Weishaupt's was **Spartacus**. Before long they settled on a grander name: the **Illuminati**, "the enlightened ones".

Their goals sound mild today: to oppose superstition, the Church's grip on public life and the abuse of state power, at a time when saying so openly could cost you your job or your freedom. The order recruited through Freemasons' lodges and grew to about 650 members that historians can verify, among them nobles, writers and officials. Weishaupt later claimed 2,500.

It didn't last. Bavaria's ruler, Elector Charles Theodore, banned secret societies in a series of edicts in 1784 and 1785. Weishaupt fled, and the authorities seized the order's papers and published them to show how dangerous it supposedly was. By the late 1780s the Bavarian Illuminati was finished.

But the legend was only beginning. In 1797 and 1798, two bestselling books, by the French priest Augustin Barruel and the Scottish physicist John Robison, claimed that the Illuminati had secretly survived and caused the French Revolution. Ever since, the name has been stuck onto almost any shadowy plot people fear, involving bankers, politicians or pop stars.

There is no evidence that the order survived its ban. The famous pyramid-and-eye on the US dollar comes from the Great Seal of the United States, designed in 1782 with no connection to the Illuminati. Today's "Illuminati" is a mix of real 18th-century history, two centuries of rumours, and a lot of internet jokes.

known: The Bavarian Illuminati was founded on 1 May 1776 by Adam Weishaupt and four students in Ingolstadt.
Its stated aims were Enlightenment ideals: opposing superstition, religious control of public life and abuses of power.
By the end of 1784 it had about 650 verifiable members; Weishaupt later claimed 2,500.
Bavaria banned secret societies in edicts of 1784 and 1785, and the order collapsed.
In 1797–98 Barruel and Robison popularised the claim that the Illuminati had survived and caused the French Revolution.
The pyramid and eye on the dollar come from the 1782 Great Seal of the United States.
speculation: **The Illuminati survived in secret.** There's no evidence of the order after the late 1780s.
**They caused the French Revolution.** Historians point to France's debt crisis, food shortages and Enlightenment ideas in general, not a Bavarian secret club.

**The eye on the dollar is their symbol.** It's the Great Seal's "Eye of Providence", a common Christian symbol at the time. The pyramid's date, MDCCLXXVI (1776), refers to the Declaration of Independence.
**Celebrities are secret members.** Hand signs, triangles and eyes in music videos are mostly marketing, in-jokes and fans playing along.

speculation.text: **They secretly control banks and governments.** There's no evidence. Some versions recycle much older conspiracy myths about Jewish people, which is one reason historians take the theory's spread seriously.

whyPeopleWonder: The Illuminati theory has a perfect starting point: **it really existed**. A secret society with code names and an owl symbol, outlawed by a king? That's a story anyone would want to continue.

It also explains a complicated world in a simple way. If wars, crashes and elections all go back to one hidden group, the world makes sense, even if it's frightening. And because the group is secret, any lack of evidence can be read as proof of how well it hides.
Today a lot of it is play. People spot "Illuminati confirmed" in everything from cartoons to album covers as a running internet joke, which keeps the name alive whether anyone believes it or not.
stories.funFact: The pyramid on the dollar bill is dated **1776** in Roman numerals (MDCCLXXVI), the same year the Illuminati was founded. But it marks the Declaration of Independence. It's a coincidence that has launched a thousand theories.
stories.depthNote: Two centuries of books, pamphlets, pop culture and memes, built on nine real years of history.

stories.hook: Thousands of people are convinced the planet is a disc ringed by a wall of ice. Some have spent real money to prove it, and accidentally proved the opposite.
stories.verdictNote: The Earth's size was measured more than 2,200 years ago, and it has been photographed from space countless times since.

story: Around 240 BC, a Greek scholar in Egypt named **Eratosthenes** noticed something. At noon on midsummer's day the Sun shone straight down a well at Syene, in the south, while in Alexandria, far to the north, it cast a shadow. Using the angle of that shadow and the distance between the cities, he worked out the size of the round Earth, and got remarkably close.

Contrary to a popular myth, educated people in the Middle Ages knew the Earth was round too. The idea that Columbus had to convince flat-Earth churchmen was largely invented in the 1800s, partly by the American writer Washington Irving.

Modern flat-Earth belief began with an Englishman, **Samuel Rowbotham**. In 1838 he watched a boat along a long, straight canal called the Bedford Level and concluded that the water wasn't curving. Writing as "Parallax", he described the world as a disc centred on the North Pole, ringed by a wall of ice: Antarctica. In 1870 the naturalist **Alfred Russel Wallace** repeated the canal experiment, correcting for the way air bends light, and showed the curve.

A Flat Earth Society was founded in 1956, but the idea really took off on YouTube in the 2010s. A 2018 YouGov poll found that about 4% of Americans believed it, and flat-Earth conferences drew paying crowds.

Every test gives the same answer. Ships disappear hull-first over the horizon, time zones exist, the Earth's shadow on the Moon during an eclipse is always round, and people have been sailing and flying all the way around the globe since 1522. Some flat-Earthers have even run their own experiments with expensive equipment, and got results showing the Earth rotates.

known: Eratosthenes measured the size of the spherical Earth around 240 BC.
Most educated medieval Europeans knew the Earth was round. The "flat-Earth Middle Ages" is a 19th-century myth.
The first circumnavigation of the globe was completed in 1522.
In 1870 Alfred Russel Wallace repeated Rowbotham's canal experiment, corrected for atmospheric refraction, and showed a curved Earth.
Shadows, time zones, eclipses, satellites and photographs from space all confirm a spherical Earth.
A 2018 YouGov poll found that around 4% of Americans believed in a flat Earth.
speculation: **The Earth is a disc ringed by an ice wall.** No one has ever found an edge. Antarctica has been crossed and circled, and southern-hemisphere flights only make sense on a globe.
**NASA fakes the photos.** Many countries and private companies photograph the Earth from space, including the USA's rivals, and they all show the same round planet.
**"Water always finds its level."** It does, but on a planet-sized scale "level" means curving around the Earth's centre of gravity.
**"We'd feel the Earth spinning."** You can't feel steady motion, which is why you don't feel a smooth plane flight at cruising speed.
**"The horizon looks flat."** The curve is too gentle to see from the ground, but it's clearly visible from high-altitude balloons and aircraft.
whyPeopleWonder: Flat-Earth belief is rarely about geography. It's about **trust**. If you already believe that governments, scientists and media lie, then the shape of the planet becomes the ultimate test: here, at least, you can "see for yourself".
It also offers community and a sense of being special: you're one of the few who has woken up. Online, video recommendation algorithms made it easy to fall from one flat-Earth clip to the next.

Psychologists note how hard it is to argue someone out of a belief that has become part of who they are. Even when experiments go against them, believers often look for a flaw in the experiment rather than in the idea.

funFact.text: In the 2018 documentary *Behind the Curve*, flat-Earthers bought a ring-laser gyroscope worth about $20,000 to prove the Earth doesn't rotate. It detected a drift of about 15 degrees per hour: exactly the Earth's rotation.

stories.hook: Look up on the right day and the sky is criss-crossed with white trails that spread into haze. Millions of people believe they're being sprayed. The trails have a much simpler story.
stories.verdictNote: The trails are ordinary contrails: water vapour from jet engines freezing into ice crystals. In a 2016 survey, 76 of 77 atmospheric experts had found no evidence of secret spraying.

story: Planes flying high leave white trails across the sky. They're called **contrails**, short for condensation trails. Jet engines burn fuel and pour out hot, humid exhaust; in the freezing air several kilometres up, that water vapour condenses and freezes into tiny ice crystals, a bit like your breath on a frosty morning.

In the late 1990s a new idea spread online: that some trails, especially the ones that linger for hours and spread into sheets of cloud, weren't contrails at all but **chemtrails**, chemicals deliberately sprayed by governments. The theory took off after a 1996 US Air Force research paper with a dramatic title, *Weather as a Force Multiplier: Owning the Weather in 2025*, and was popularised on late-night radio by Art Bell from 1999.

Believers suggest many purposes: controlling the weather, dimming the Sun, controlling the population, or making people ill. Photos of rows of barrels inside aircraft cabins were shared as proof of spraying equipment.

The science is straightforward. Whether a contrail vanishes in seconds or lasts for hours depends on how cold and humid the air is at that height. In dry air the ice crystals quickly turn back into vapour; in moist air they persist and spread into cirrus-like cloud. Those barrels hold water, used to imitate the weight of passengers on test flights. And the Air Force paper described its scenarios as fictional, an imagined future rather than a programme.

In 2016, researchers asked 77 leading atmospheric chemists and geochemists to examine the "evidence" chemtrail believers cite. 76 said they had found no sign of a secret spraying programme, and that the claims could be explained by normal contrails and poor sampling. Real proposals to dim sunlight to cool the planet, called solar geoengineering, do exist, but they are debated openly by scientists, not secretly sprayed on you.

known: Contrails are mostly ice crystals formed when water vapour in engine exhaust condenses and freezes in very cold air.
How long a contrail lasts depends on the temperature and humidity at cruising altitude. In humid air they can last for hours and spread into cirrus-like cloud.
The 1996 Air Force paper described future scenarios as fictional. In 2005 the Air Force said it had no weather-modification programmes.
Federal agencies published a joint explanation of contrails in 2000.
In a 2016 study, 76 of 77 atmospheric chemists and geochemists said they had found no evidence of a secret spraying programme.
The barrels seen in cabin photos are water tanks used to simulate passenger weight on test flights.
speculation: **Lingering trails must be chemicals.** Persistence depends on humidity at altitude, which is why trails behave differently from day to day.
**It's secret weather control.** The 1996 paper was a speculative scenario. Cloud seeding does exist, but it's done openly, locally, and isn't what you see from airliners.
**It's population control, or making people ill.** No difference in chemistry between "chemtrails" and contrails has ever been shown.
**Soil and water samples prove it.** The tests cited have been flawed, or measured normal levels of naturally occurring elements.

**Solar geoengineering is already happening in secret.** Proposals exist and are debated publicly, and even small outdoor tests are controversial. There's no evidence of a secret large-scale programme.
whyPeopleWonder: Chemtrails are a conspiracy theory you can *see*. Once someone points out the crossing lines in the sky, you notice them everywhere, and busy flight routes make criss-cross patterns over many cities. Psychologists call this the **frequency illusion**: once something is on your mind, you spot it all the time.

There's also a real kernel. Governments have experimented with weather modification, and scientists do discuss deliberately cooling the planet. Those real topics make the leap to "they're already doing it" feel small.
And it taps into a deep fear: that something invisible is being done to us without consent. That fear tends to grow when trust in governments and experts is low.
stories.funFact: Those famous photos of rows of barrels inside a plane? They're water tanks for test flights. Engineers pump water from barrel to barrel to see how the aircraft handles as its balance shifts.
stories.depthNote: Plenty of videos and photos online, but the explanation is simple physics.

story: In the autumn of 1969, a strange rumour swept American college campuses: Paul McCartney of the Beatles was dead. He had supposedly died in a car crash in late 1966, and the band, desperate to spare fans the grief, had replaced him with the winner of a McCartney lookalike contest. Guilt-ridden, the story went, the surviving Beatles had been hiding clues to the truth in their songs and album covers ever since.

Rumours about Paul's health had floated around since 1966. But in September 1969 a student newspaper at Drake University in Iowa printed an article asking "Is Beatle Paul McCartney Dead?". On 12 October a caller to Detroit DJ **Russ Gibb**'s radio show laid out the "clues", and Gibb and his listeners spent the next hour finding more. Two days later a University of Michigan student, **Fred LaBour**, published a joke review of the new album *Abbey Road* listing clue after clue, many of which he later admitted he'd simply made up.

Fans went wild for clue-hunting. Play "Revolution 9" backwards, they said, and you'd hear "turn me on, dead man". On the *Abbey Road* cover, Paul is barefoot and out of step with the others, like a corpse in a funeral procession: John in white as the preacher, Ringo in black as the undertaker, George in denim as the gravedigger. A parked Volkswagen's number plate seemed to read "28IF", Paul's age *if* he'd lived. (He was actually 27, and the plate said LMW 281F.)

By late October it was international news, and the Beatles' office was flooded with calls. Ringo told one reporter: "If people are gonna believe it, they're gonna believe it. I can only say it's not true." Meanwhile, McCartney had simply retreated with his young family to his farm in Scotland, which only deepened the mystery.

In November 1969 *Life* magazine tracked him down. "Perhaps the rumour started because I haven't been much in the press lately," he said. The rumour faded, though it never quite died. In 1993 McCartney released a live album called *Paul Is Live*, its cover a playful parody of *Abbey Road*.

known: Paul McCartney was born in 1942 and is alive.
The rumour began in 1966 but exploded in September and October 1969, spread by student papers and radio DJs.
Fred LaBour later said he had invented many of the clues in his joke review.
The "OPD" ("Officially Pronounced Dead") badge on the *Sgt. Pepper* sleeve actually reads "OPP", for Ontario Provincial Police.
The VW's plate reads LMW 281F, not "28IF", and McCartney was 27 when *Abbey Road* came out.
Lennon said he wrote "the Walrus was Paul" partly to tease people who hunted for hidden meanings.
speculation: **The Abbey Road cover is a funeral procession.** It's a photo of four men crossing a road, taken quickly outside their studio. Meaning was read into it afterwards.
**Backwards messages reveal the truth.** The Beatles did experiment with reversed sounds, but hearing words in noise is a well-known trick of the brain, called pareidolia.
**The replacement was "William Campbell" or "Billy Shears".** The Campbell name came from LaBour's joke review; Billy Shears is a character in a *Sgt. Pepper* song.
**MI5 arranged the swap.** There's no evidence at all.
**The Beatles started it as a publicity stunt.** Lennon said the rumour was good publicity for *Abbey Road*, but there's no evidence the band created it.
whyPeopleWonder: Timing mattered. In 1969 many young Americans distrusted authority because of the Vietnam War. As the student who wrote the first article later put it, they were ready to believe just about any conspiracy.

The Beatles were also treated almost like prophets. Fans studied every lyric and cover for personal messages, so a game of finding hidden clues felt natural, and it was fun. Our brains are pattern-finding machines: give them enough records and photos and they'll find a story.
Finally, McCartney really had gone quiet, hiding away on a Scottish farm while the band was quietly falling apart. A real absence plus a good story is a powerful mix.
stories.funFact: As the rumour peaked, singer José Feliciano released a cash-in single called "So Long Paul" under the made-up name Werbley Finster. Other records included "We're All Paul Bearers".
stories.depthNote: A fun clue-hunting game more than a deep mystery, but people have written whole books of "evidence".

stories.title: The Death of *Diana*
stories.hook: In the early hours of 31 August 1997, a car carrying Diana, Princess of Wales, crashed in a Paris tunnel. The world's most photographed woman was dead at 36, and the questions began almost at once.
stories.verdictNote: French and British investigations found no evidence of murder. In 2008 an inquest jury ruled it an unlawful killing caused by the grossly negligent driving of the chauffeur and the pursuing vehicles.

story: Shortly after midnight on 31 August 1997, Diana, Princess of Wales, and her partner **Dodi Fayed** slipped out of the back of the Ritz Hotel in Paris, trying to avoid the photographers waiting at the front. Their driver, **Henri Paul**, the hotel's deputy head of security, sped off in a black Mercedes along the River Seine. At 12:23 am, at the entrance to the Pont de l'Alma underpass, he lost control. The car clipped a white Fiat Uno and hit a concrete pillar head-on.

Dodi Fayed and Henri Paul were killed. Diana was taken to the Pitié-Salpêtrière Hospital, where she died at 4 am. Her bodyguard, **Trevor Rees-Jones**, was the only survivor, badly injured. The car had been travelling at about 105 km/h, more than twice the tunnel's speed limit, and no one inside was wearing a seat belt.

Grief swept the world: her funeral was watched by an estimated 2.5 billion people. And because the story involved the royal family, secret services, a famous billionaire and a mystery car that was never traced, theories soon followed. The loudest voice was Dodi's father, **Mohamed Al-Fayed**, owner of Harrods and the Ritz, who for years claimed the couple had been murdered by MI6 on the royal family's orders.

The claims were examined in detail. A French investigation in 1999 found that Henri Paul was drunk, with a blood-alcohol level more than three times the French limit, had taken prescription drugs, and lost control at high speed. A British police inquiry led by Lord Stevens, **Operation Paget**, reported in 2006 and found no evidence of a conspiracy. In 2008, after six months of hearings and some 250 witnesses, an inquest jury returned a verdict of **unlawful killing**, caused by the grossly negligent driving of Henri Paul and of the following vehicles.

A few threads were never tied up: the driver of the white Fiat Uno was never conclusively identified. But no evidence has ever shown the crash was anything other than a tragic, avoidable accident, made worse by speed, alcohol, the chase, and seat belts left unbuckled.

known: The crash happened at 12:23 am on 31 August 1997. Diana died at 4 am; Dodi Fayed and Henri Paul died too. Bodyguard Trevor Rees-Jones survived.
The car was travelling at about 105 km/h in a 50 km/h tunnel.
Henri Paul's blood-alcohol level was 180 mg per 100 ml, about 3.6 times the French legal limit, and he had taken antidepressants.
None of the car's occupants was wearing a seat belt.
The Mercedes touched a white Fiat Uno whose driver was never conclusively traced.

speculation: **MI6 killed her on royal orders.** Mohamed Al-Fayed's claim. It was dismissed by the French investigation and by Operation Paget, and rejected by the inquest jury's verdict.

speculation.text: **She was pregnant, or about to announce an engagement.** Both claims were examined by Britain's police inquiry, Operation Paget. Tests showed she was not pregnant, and every conspiracy allegation was found to be without foundation.

**The white Fiat was part of a plot.** The Mercedes did touch a white Fiat Uno in the tunnel, and its driver was never conclusively traced. A photographer who had followed Diana that week, James Andanson, attracted suspicion, but no evidence ever linked him to a plot.

speculation: **A blinding flash caused the crash.** Some witnesses mentioned a flash. Investigators found no evidence of a deliberate light being used.
**Henri Paul was secretly paid by intelligence agents.** The inquest examined the money in his accounts and found no evidence of a plot.
whyPeopleWonder: Diana was loved by millions, and her death felt impossible: the most famous woman in the world, killed in an ordinary car crash. The mind rebels against that, and a hidden plot can feel more fitting than a drunk driver and an unbuckled seat belt.
Her relationship with the royal family was famously troubled, and she had spoken about feeling watched and under threat. That made a sinister explanation feel plausible to many people.

And one very rich, very determined man spent a decade insisting it was murder. Mohamed Al-Fayed's grief and resources kept the theory in the headlines long after the evidence had settled the question.
stories.funFact: Elton John's rewritten "Candle in the Wind 1997", performed at Diana's funeral, became the best-selling single since the UK and US charts began in the 1950s, with sales of more than 33 million copies.
stories.depthNote: Years of investigations, a six-month inquest and endless tabloid theories, but the official findings are clear.

stories.title: COVID-19 *Origins*
stories.hook: A new coronavirus surfaced in Wuhan, China, in late 2019 and went on to kill millions. Did it come from a wildlife market or a laboratory a few miles away? The argument still isn't over.
stories.verdictNote: Neither origin is proven. Most scientists who study it think a natural spillover from animals is more likely; a lab accident hasn't been ruled out, and some intelligence agencies lean that way with low confidence. There's no evidence it was made as a weapon.

story: In December 2019, doctors in Wuhan, a central Chinese city of more than 10 million people, began seeing clusters of a mysterious pneumonia. Many of the first known patients were linked to the **Huanan Seafood Wholesale Market**, where live wild animals were sold alongside seafood. Within weeks the new coronavirus, later named SARS-CoV-2, was spreading around the world.

There are two main ideas about where it came from, and both are taken seriously by at least some experts. The first is **natural spillover**: a bat virus passed to another animal and then to people, probably through the wildlife trade, as happened with the first SARS outbreak in 2002–04. The second is a **lab leak**: Wuhan is also home to the Wuhan Institute of Virology, which collected and studied bat coronaviruses, and an accident there could in theory have let one escape.

The evidence for the market: early cases clustered around it, and two studies published in *Science* in 2022 found that virus-positive samples were concentrated where live animals such as raccoon dogs were sold. The closest known relatives of the virus come from horseshoe bats in Laos and Yunnan. The case for a lab leak is mostly circumstantial: the lab's location, its research on related viruses, and Chinese secrecy, including refusing international audits of its labs.

Official verdicts are split and cautious. A 2021 WHO–China study called a lab leak "extremely unlikely", but the WHO's own director-general said that conclusion was premature. US intelligence agencies disagree with each other, mostly with low confidence: the FBI leans towards a lab leak with moderate confidence, while others lean towards a natural origin. In 2025 the WHO's scientific advisory group said the weight of available evidence points to a natural, zoonotic origin, but that the question can't be settled without more data from China.

What clearly *isn't* supported is the most extreme version: that the virus was engineered as a weapon and released on purpose. The debate has also been poisoned by politics, at times used to stoke hostility towards Chinese people. A 2024 survey of 168 experts, mostly epidemiologists and virologists, found that on average they rated a natural spillover 77% likely and a lab leak 21% likely. In other words: probably nature, but not certain.

speculation: **Natural spillover at the market.** The view most scientists favour, supported by where the early cases and positive samples were. But the infected animal has never been found.

**An accidental lab leak.** Taken seriously by some scientists and agencies. There's no direct evidence: no record of the virus in any lab before the outbreak, and the lab says its staff tested negative.
**The virus was engineered.** Claims based on features of its genome, such as its furin cleavage site, are disputed; the scientific consensus is that it isn't genetically engineered.
**It was a bioweapon released on purpose.** No evidence. The idea spread from fringe websites in early 2020.

**Scientists covered it up.** A prominent scientist who organised an early statement dismissing the lab theory didn't disclose his links to the Wuhan lab. That damaged trust, but it doesn't prove where the virus came from.
whyPeopleWonder: This is the rare case where "unproven" cuts both ways. The coincidence is real: a novel bat coronavirus emerged in the same city as a leading bat-coronavirus lab. It's natural to ask the question, and asking it isn't a conspiracy theory.

Secrecy makes it worse. China restricted access to early data, samples and labs, and some scientists' early, confident dismissals of the lab idea, plus undisclosed conflicts of interest, damaged public trust in the experts.

And the stakes are enormous. A pandemic that killed millions and changed everyone's lives *feels* like it needs someone to blame. Politics then turned a scientific question into a team sport, which makes careful, uncertain answers harder to hear.
stories.funFact: In 2026, scientists compared how SARS-CoV-2 mutated in its early days with five natural outbreaks and with the 1977 "Russian flu", which probably came from a lab. COVID's pattern matched the natural outbreaks, not the lab one.
stories.depthNote: Bottomless. Genomes, intelligence reports, leaked emails, WHO studies and fierce scientific and political fights, all still unfolding.

story: On the afternoon of 5 December 1945, five US Navy torpedo bombers took off from Fort Lauderdale, Florida, on a routine training flight. Known as **Flight 19**, they carried 14 airmen. A couple of hours later the flight leader radioed that his compasses weren't working and he couldn't tell where they were. The planes were never found.

That evening a large flying boat went out to search for them, with 13 men aboard. It vanished too, although a passing ship reported seeing flames on the water. Two aircraft, 27 men, no wreckage. The story was too strange to forget.

Over the next decades writers began connecting it to other losses in the same waters, such as the giant Navy cargo ship USS *Cyclops*, which disappeared with 306 people aboard in 1918. In 1964 a magazine writer, Vincent Gaddis, gave the area a name: **the Bermuda Triangle**. Ten years later, a bestselling book blamed everything from time warps to the lost city of Atlantis.

Then a librarian named Larry Kusche did something nobody had bothered to do: he checked the original records. In his 1975 book he showed that many famous "mysteries" had ordinary explanations, had happened in bad storms, or had taken place hundreds of miles away. A few had never happened at all.

Today the US Coast Guard and the big shipping insurers don't treat the area as unusually dangerous. It's one of the busiest stretches of ocean on Earth, crossed by the powerful Gulf Stream and regular storms and hurricanes. With that much traffic, accidents are expected, and the deep water can make wreckage very hard to find.

known: The "Triangle" has no official boundaries, and US authorities don't recognise it as a special danger zone.
The area is one of the busiest shipping and flight routes in the world, with the fast Gulf Stream current and frequent storms.

known.text: Lloyd's of London found that unusually large numbers of ships have not sunk there, and it doesn't charge higher rates to cross it.

Flight 19's leader believed they were over the Florida Keys when they were probably far to the north-east. The planes most likely ran out of fuel and ditched at night in rough seas. The Navy later changed the official cause to "unknown" after the flight leader's mother objected.

known: Investigator Larry Kusche found that many famous Triangle cases were exaggerated, happened elsewhere, or never happened.
The name comes from a 1964 magazine article, not from sailors or official sources.
speculation: **Atlantis's lost energy crystals.** Based on the psychic Edgar Cayce's readings. There's no evidence Atlantis existed.
**Methane gas erupting from the seabed** and sinking ships. It's possible in theory, but there's no evidence of large recent eruptions in this area.
**Rogue waves.** Giant waves are real and could sink ships, but they happen in oceans all over the world.
**Magnetic weirdness that confuses compasses.** Compass variation exists everywhere, and navigators routinely correct for it.
**Aliens or time warps.** No evidence at all.
whyPeopleWonder: A great name does a lot of work. Once a region is called *the Bermuda Triangle*, every accident inside it becomes part of a pattern, while accidents just outside it are forgotten. Psychologists call this the **clustering illusion**: seeing meaningful groups in random events.

Disappearances without wreckage are especially haunting. Our minds hate open endings. Parts of the area are deep ocean, so wreckage can sink thousands of metres and be very hard to find, and "we found nothing" easily turns into "something took them".
Books, documentaries and films kept the legend alive because it's a fantastic story. Correcting a good story is always harder than telling one.

funFact.text: Flight 19's lost Avengers make a surprise appearance in Steven Spielberg's *Close Encounters of the Third Kind* (1977), where the missing planes are found, good as new, in the Sonoran Desert.

stories.depthNote: A handful of real tragedies, buried under fifty years of embellishment. Easy to dig out once you check the records.

stories.title: Amelia *Earhart*
stories.hook: The most famous pilot in the world set out to fly around the globe in 1937. With 7,000 miles to go, she and her navigator vanished over the Pacific.
stories.verdictNote: Most experts think the plane ran out of fuel and sank near Howland Island. A rival theory says they landed on a remote reef. No wreckage has ever been confirmed.

story: By 1937 Amelia Earhart was one of the most famous people on Earth. In 1932 she had become the first woman to fly solo, nonstop across the Atlantic. Now she wanted to be the first woman to fly around the world, taking a long route near the equator in a twin-engine Lockheed Electra, with the experienced navigator **Fred Noonan**.

By 29 June they had reached Lae, in New Guinea, with about 22,000 miles behind them and 7,000 to go, nearly all of it over open ocean. The hardest leg came next: a long flight to **Howland Island**, a tiny, flat speck of land in the middle of the Pacific, where the US Coast Guard ship *Itasca* waited to guide them in by radio.

On the morning of 2 July the *Itasca*'s radio operators heard Earhart's voice, strong and clear. She reported that they should be near the island but couldn't see it, and that fuel was running low. But she couldn't hear the ship's replies, and attempts to take a radio bearing on her plane failed. Her last confirmed message gave a navigation line, "157 337", and then there was silence.
The US Navy and Coast Guard launched an enormous air and sea search. Nothing was found, and in January 1939 Earhart was declared legally dead.

Ever since, people have argued over what happened. The simplest explanation, known as "crash and sink", is that they ran out of fuel near Howland and went down in very deep water. Another popular theory says they landed on the reef of **Nikumaroro**, a remote, uninhabited atoll to the south, and died there as castaways. Bones found on the island in 1940 were judged at the time to be a man's, then reassessed in 2018 as consistent with Earhart. Expeditions keep searching. None has found the plane.

known: Earhart and Noonan disappeared on 2 July 1937 while flying from Lae, New Guinea, to Howland Island in a Lockheed Electra 10E.
The Coast Guard cutter *Itasca* received her voice transmissions clearly, but she could not hear the ship, and radio direction-finding failed.
Her last confirmed message reported a line of position, 157–337.
A large US Navy and Coast Guard search found nothing, and she was declared legally dead on 5 January 1939.
Thirteen bones found on Nikumaroro in 1940 were judged male at the time, then reassessed in 2018 as consistent with Earhart. The bones themselves are not available to test.
Searches by Robert Ballard (2019) and others (2024) found no wreckage.
speculation: **They crashed and sank near Howland ("crash and sink").** The view of many experts: low on fuel, unable to find the island, they ditched in deep ocean. It fits the evidence but hasn't been proven, because the plane has never been found.
**They landed on Nikumaroro and died as castaways.** Supported by the 1940 bones, some artefacts and possible distress calls. Debated, and no aircraft wreckage has been found.

speculation.text: **They were captured by the Japanese.** Based mostly on later witness accounts from the Marshall Islands and Saipan. A 2017 "photo of Earhart in captivity" turned out to come from a Japanese travel book published in 1935, two years before she vanished.

speculation: **She survived and lived under a new name.** The claim that she became Irene Bolam was denied by Bolam, who sued; the book was withdrawn.
**She was on a spy mission.** A popular idea, but no evidence has been found in US or Japanese records.
whyPeopleWonder: Earhart wasn't just a pilot. She was a symbol of courage and of what women could do, and people didn't want her story to end with a quiet splash in an empty ocean. It's natural to hope she made it somewhere.

The mystery is also full of tantalising near-misses: radio calls that were heard but not answered, a reef that might have been within range, bones that were measured and then lost. Each clue seems so close to an answer.
And new technology keeps reopening the case. Better sonar, forensic software and satellite images all promise that *this* expedition will be the one.

funFact.text: In April 1933 Amelia Earhart and First Lady Eleanor Roosevelt slipped away from a White House dinner, still in their evening gowns, to take a night flight over Washington, D.C.

stories.hook: A polite man in a dark suit hijacked a jet, collected $200,000, and jumped out of the back into a stormy night. He was never seen again.

story: It was the afternoon before Thanksgiving, 24 November 1971. At Portland airport a quiet man in a dark suit and tie bought a one-way ticket to Seattle under the name **Dan Cooper**. He ordered a bourbon and 7-Up, and soon after take-off handed a flight attendant a note. She assumed he was flirting and put it in her pocket. He leaned over and told her she'd better read it: he had a bomb.

He opened his briefcase just enough to show wires and red cylinders, and made his demands: $200,000 in cash and four parachutes. In Seattle the airline handed them over, and he let the other 35 passengers go. Then he ordered the plane back into the air, heading for Mexico, low and slow, with the rear stairs unlocked.

Somewhere over the dark, rainy forests of south-west Washington, around 8 pm, the crew felt the tail bump. When the jet landed in Reno, the hijacker was gone. He had jumped from the rear stairs in a business suit and loafers, into freezing rain, at night, with $200,000 strapped to him.

The FBI launched one of the biggest manhunts in its history. A reporter's mix-up gave the hijacker the name **"D.B. Cooper"**, and it stuck. Thousands of tips came in, and hundreds of suspects were considered. Then, in 1980, an eight-year-old boy digging on a sandy bank of the Columbia River found bundles of rotted $20 bills. Their serial numbers matched the ransom.

That was the last real breakthrough. Nobody knows how the money got to that beach, and the other $194,000 or so has never turned up. In 2016 the FBI closed its active investigation. The bureau has long suspected that Cooper didn't survive the jump, but nobody can prove it.

known: On 24 November 1971 a man calling himself Dan Cooper hijacked a Boeing 727 and demanded $200,000 and four parachutes.
The FBI recorded the serial numbers of all 10,000 $20 bills before handing them over.
He jumped from the plane's rear stairs at night in bad weather over rough, forested country.
"D.B. Cooper" was never his alias: the initials came from a press mix-up with an early, cleared suspect.
In 1980, $5,800 of the ransom was found on a Columbia River beach. How it got there is still debated.
He left behind a clip-on tie, which was later tested for DNA and microscopic particles.
The FBI considered hundreds of suspects and never charged anyone.
speculation: **He died in the jump.** The FBI's long-time view: a parachute jump at night, in rain, over forest, in a suit and loafers, would be deadly for anyone but an expert.
**He survived and spent the money.** Possible, but none of the other marked bills has ever turned up anywhere.

speculation.text: **Richard McCoy did it.** Five months later he carried out a strikingly similar hijacking. But the FBI doesn't consider him a suspect, because his age and looks didn't match: McCoy was 29, while witnesses put Cooper in his mid-40s.

speculation: **He had military or aviation training.** His knowledge of the 727's rear stairs suggests some aviation background, but that's an inference, not evidence.
**The money was planted.** Some think the 1980 cash was buried or washed to Tena Bar by floods or dredging. Experts disagree, and none of it proves where Cooper landed.
whyPeopleWonder: Cooper is the rare criminal who became a folk hero. He was calm and polite, he robbed an airline rather than a person, and he simply disappeared. People love a clever underdog, and they love a story where the system loses.

The case is also a real puzzle you can work on yourself, with maps, wind speeds, serial numbers, and a tie full of particles. Amateur sleuths have spent decades on it, and every few years someone announces they've finally cracked it.
Most of all, the ending is missing. Our brains are wired to want to close loops. A man jumps into the dark and the story just... stops. That gap is irresistible.

stories.title: Jack the *Ripper*
stories.hook: In the autumn of 1888 a killer stalked the poorest streets of London's East End. He was never caught, and even his famous nickname was probably invented by a journalist.
stories.verdictNote: Despite more than a century of "case closed" books and a long list of named suspects, the killer has never been identified, and there's no confirmed forensic evidence left to test.

story: In 1888, Whitechapel in London's East End was one of the poorest places in Britain. Around 80,000 people crowded its streets; thousands slept in common lodging houses each night, paying fourpence for a bed. Between August and November that year, five women were murdered there in a series of killings so brutal and so widely reported that they created a legend.

The five, **Mary Ann "Polly" Nichols, Annie Chapman, Elizabeth Stride, Catherine Eddowes and Mary Jane Kelly**, are known as the "canonical five". Police investigated eleven murders in the area between 1888 and 1891, and historians still debate which were by the same hand.

The famous name came from a letter. In late September 1888 a news agency received a taunting note signed "Jack the Ripper". It's widely believed to have been a hoax, perhaps written by a journalist to sell papers. Hundreds more letters followed. One, the "From Hell" letter sent to George Lusk of the Whitechapel Vigilance Committee, arrived with half of a preserved human kidney.

Detectives such as Inspector Frederick Abberline threw themselves into the case, but without fingerprinting, forensic science or modern records they were working almost blind. In 1894 a senior officer, Sir Melville Macnaghten, wrote a memo naming three men he thought more likely than others: Montague Druitt, Aaron Kosminski and Michael Ostrog. None was ever charged, and the memo contains factual errors.

Since then, writers have accused more than a hundred people, from a Polish barber to a royal prince to the painter Walter Sickert. Some have claimed DNA proof, but the samples and methods have been heavily criticised. Meanwhile, historian Hallie Rubenhold's prize-winning 2019 book *The Five* turned attention back to the women themselves: their lives, families and struggles, rather than the man who killed them.

known: Five women were murdered in Whitechapel and Spitalfields between 31 August and 9 November 1888: the "canonical five".
Police investigated eleven murders in the area between April 1888 and February 1891 as the "Whitechapel murders".
The name "Jack the Ripper" first appeared in the "Dear Boss" letter, widely believed to be a hoax.
The "From Hell" letter, sent to George Lusk on 16 October 1888, came with half a preserved human kidney.
In 1894 Sir Melville Macnaghten named Druitt, Kosminski and Ostrog as suspects, but his memo contains factual errors and he only joined the police after the murders.
No confirmed forensic evidence survives. Modern DNA claims have been heavily criticised.
speculation: **Aaron Kosminski**, a Polish barber committed to an asylum in 1891. Named by Macnaghten and by Chief Inspector Swanson. A 2014 DNA claim is widely doubted.
**Montague Druitt**, a barrister who drowned himself in December 1888. Inspector Abberline thought the case against him rested only on the timing of his death, and he lived across the river in Kent.

speculation.text: **Walter Sickert**, the painter, accused by Patricia Cornwell in 2002. Most Ripper historians reject the case: strong evidence shows he was in France during most of the murders.

**Prince Albert Victor**, Queen Victoria's grandson. The rumour first appeared in print in 1962, but royal records place him far from London: on the night of the double murder he was at Balmoral in Scotland.

speculation: **Francis Tumblety**, an Irish-American quack "herb doctor" who was in London in 1888. Intriguing, but there's no direct evidence.
whyPeopleWonder: Jack the Ripper was the first serial killer of the mass-media age. Cheap newspapers, sensational drawings and hoax letters turned the murders into a story that sold, and the story has been retold ever since.

An anonymous killer is a blank screen. Writers can project anyone onto it, from a mad doctor to a royal, and because everyone involved died long ago, nobody can answer back. That makes for endless new "solutions".

But the legend has a cost. The murders were real crimes against real, poor women, and the fascination with the killer long overshadowed the victims. In recent years historians have pushed back, asking who these women were, not just who killed them.

stories.depthNote: Bottomless. A century of books, a field of its own ("Ripperology"), and hundreds of named suspects.

stories.hook: A killer terrorised California in 1968 and 1969, then taunted police and newspapers with letters and secret codes. One cipher took 51 years to crack. His name is still unknown.

story: Between December 1968 and October 1969, a killer attacked seven people in four separate attacks around the San Francisco Bay Area: two teenagers on a lovers' lane outside Benicia, a young couple in a Vallejo car park, two students at Lake Berryessa, and a taxi driver in San Francisco. Five died. Two survived.

Then the killer started writing. Letters arrived at Bay Area newspapers boasting of the murders, giving details only the police knew, and demanding to be printed on the front page or more people would die. One began, "This is the Zodiac speaking." They were signed with a symbol like the crosshairs of a gunsight.

Some letters contained ciphers. The first, a 408-symbol code split between three newspapers, was cracked within days in August 1969 by Donald and Bettye Harden, a couple in Salinas, neither of them professional codebreakers. Bettye guessed that the word "kill" would appear. It did.

The most famous, the **340-character cipher**, held out for 51 years. In December 2020 three amateur codebreakers, an American software engineer, an Australian mathematician and a Belgian programmer, finally solved it after a computer program tested some 650,000 possible solutions. It didn't reveal his name. Two very short ciphers remain unsolved, and may be impossible to crack with any certainty.

The Zodiac's last confirmed letter arrived in 1974. Police have considered thousands of suspects. The only one they ever named, a former teacher called **Arthur Leigh Allen**, was never charged and died in 1992, and a partial DNA profile from the letters didn't match him. The case has inspired films from *Dirty Harry* to David Fincher's *Zodiac*, and amateur detectives around the world still hunt for the answer.

known: The Zodiac attacked seven people on four occasions in 1968–69. Five died and two survived.
From 1969 to 1974 he sent more than twenty letters to newspapers, police, a reporter and a lawyer.
He sent four ciphers. The 408 was solved in 1969 and the 340 in 2020; two short ones remain unsolved.
Arthur Leigh Allen is the only suspect police ever named. He denied it, was never charged, and died in 1992.
A partial DNA profile from the letters (2002) didn't match Allen, though some researchers question whether it came from the killer.
The case remains open with the FBI, the California Department of Justice and several local agencies.
speculation: **Arthur Leigh Allen was the Zodiac.** He was investigated for twenty years. Lead investigator Dave Toschi said in 2010 that all the evidence against him ultimately "turned out to be negative".
**Another named suspect.** Enthusiasts have argued for Earl Van Best Jr., Gary Francis Poste, Richard Gaikowski and others. None has been proven, and police say new suspects are named every year.
**He knew Darlene Ferrin.** Author Robert Graysmith argued for a connection. It has never been proven.
**He killed 37 people.** His own claim in 1974. Investigators confirm five murders.
**The short ciphers hide his name.** Hundreds of solutions have been proposed, but they're so short that it's practically impossible to tell if any is correct.
whyPeopleWonder: The Zodiac turned his crimes into a public game. By sending ciphers to newspapers, he invited everyone to play detective, and people have been playing ever since.

The case also has real clues you can study yourself: letters, handwriting, ciphers, sketches. When three amateurs cracked the 340 cipher in 2020, it proved that ordinary people with computers really can make progress where experts failed.
And like every great unsolved case, the ending is missing. The killer simply stopped writing in 1974 and vanished into history, leaving a question that refuses to close.
stories.funFact: The FBI and the CIA both tried to crack the Zodiac's first cipher in 1969. It was solved within days by a Salinas couple, Donald and Bettye Harden, neither of whom was a cryptologist.

stories.title: Flight *MH370*
stories.hook: A Boeing 777 with 239 people aboard said "Good night" to air traffic control and vanished. Satellites showed it kept flying for hours, into one of the most remote oceans on Earth.
stories.verdictNote: Debris proves the flight ended in the Indian Ocean, but the main wreckage, and the reason it turned back, have never been found. The latest search ended in January 2026 without success.

story: Shortly after midnight on 8 March 2014, Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 left Kuala Lumpur for Beijing with 227 passengers and 12 crew. About 38 minutes later, as it was handed over from Malaysian to Vietnamese air traffic control over the South China Sea, the cockpit said its last words: **"Good night. Malaysian three seven zero."** Minutes later, the plane disappeared from air-traffic radar.

It hadn't crashed. Malaysian military radar tracked it for another hour as it turned sharply back west, crossed the Malay Peninsula and flew out over the Andaman Sea, until it left radar range. After that, the only clues were a series of automatic electronic "handshakes" between the plane and an Inmarsat satellite, which showed that it kept flying for hours more.

Analysis of those signals pointed to a final position far to the south, in the remote southern Indian Ocean west of Australia. The hunt became the most expensive search in aviation history. Ships mapped 120,000 square kilometres of seabed, found nothing, and the official search was suspended in January 2017. The private company Ocean Infinity searched on a "no find, no fee" basis in 2018 and again in 2025–26; its latest attempt ended on 23 January 2026, still without success.

The ocean did give something back. In July 2015, a piece of wing called a flaperon washed up on Réunion, an island near Madagascar, and was confirmed to be from MH370. More pieces turned up on the shores of Africa and Indian Ocean islands, many found by an American amateur searcher, Blaine Gibson.

But *why* did it fly there? Investigators couldn't say. Australia's search agency first thought a loss of cabin oxygen leaving everyone unconscious fitted the data; others suspect deliberate action by someone on board. Malaysia's 2018 final report was inconclusive. For the families of the 239 people aboard, the hardest part is still not knowing.

known: MH370 carried 227 passengers (153 of them Chinese citizens) and 12 Malaysian crew.
Its last voice transmission was "Good night. Malaysian three seven zero" at 1:19 am.
Military radar tracked it turning back west across the Malay Peninsula until 2:22 am.
Automatic satellite handshakes show it flew on for hours, ending in the southern Indian Ocean.
From 2015, debris washed ashore in the western Indian Ocean; the Réunion flaperon was confirmed to be from MH370.

speculation.text: **Deliberate action by the captain.** Some experts think so. In 2016 it was reported that the FBI found a route on the captain's home flight simulator resembling a southern Indian Ocean path. No motive or proof has ever been established.

speculation: **A "ghost flight".** Australia's search agency initially thought that loss of oxygen (hypoxia) leaving everyone unconscious best fitted the data, with the plane flying on until its fuel ran out.
**A hijacking.** Considered by investigators, but no one ever claimed responsibility.
**Something in the cargo.** Investigators examined consignments including lithium-ion batteries and fruit, and questioned handlers to rule out sabotage.
**It landed somewhere secret, or was shot down.** No evidence, and debris confirms it ended in the Indian Ocean.
whyPeopleWonder: We assume a modern airliner can never just disappear. Phones are tracked, planes show up on apps. MH370 broke that assumption, and the gap between "that's impossible" and "it happened" is where theories grow.
The data that exists is strange and partial: a deliberate-looking turn, a transponder going silent, hours of satellite pings with no voice. Each fact invites a story, and none settles it.
Above all, there's no ending for the 239 families. Without wreckage or recorders, no one can tell them what happened in those last hours.
stories.funFact: The underwater locator beacon on MH370's flight data recorder had a battery that expired in 2012, more than a year before the flight. Since MH370, aviation rules have been tightened: longer-lasting beacon batteries, longer cockpit recordings and better position reporting over the open ocean.
stories.depthNote: Bottomless. Satellite maths, ocean-drift models, debris, official reports and a huge online community of analysts.

stories.hook: Nine experienced hikers cut their way out of their own tent and walked into a freezing Siberian night. None came back.
stories.verdictNote: A slab avalanche is now the leading explanation, and Russian prosecutors backed it in 2020. Not everyone is convinced.

story: Picture a search party trudging across a bare, wind-blasted mountainside in February 1959. They find a tent half-buried in snow. It hasn't been ripped open by wind. It has been **cut open from the inside**. Leading away from it are footprints of eight or nine people, most of them in socks, a single boot, or bare feet, heading downhill into a night that was probably colder than −25 °C.

The tent belonged to a group of experienced hikers, mostly students and graduates of the Ural Polytechnic Institute, led by 23-year-old Igor Dyatlov. They were attempting a tough ski trek rated Category III, the hardest grade at the time, toward a mountain called Otorten. Ten set out. One of them, Yuri Yudin, felt ill and turned back on 28 January. That decision made him the only survivor. On 1 February the other nine pitched camp on the open slope of Kholat Syakhl, a name usually translated from the Mansi language as "Dead Mountain".

The discoveries got stranger the further the searchers went. About 1.5 km downhill, under a big cedar tree, two of the men lay beside the remains of a small fire, dressed only in underwear. Three more, including Dyatlov, were found on the slope between the cedar and the tent, as if they had been trying to get back. The last four were not found until May, under deep snow in a ravine. Some of them had terrible injuries, including a fractured skull and crushed ribs, with surprisingly little damage to the skin. Traces of radioactivity turned up on some of their clothing.

In May 1959 Soviet investigators closed the case with a famously vague verdict: the hikers had died because of a **"compelling natural force"**. A secretive Cold War state plus a mystery that vague was a perfect recipe for theories, and people supplied plenty: secret weapons tests, an angry yeti, infrasound, UFOs, even a KGB operation.

Here's the twist. In 2019 Russian prosecutors reopened the case, and in 2020 they concluded that a snow slab avalanche and poor visibility drove the group out. In 2021 two scientists, Johan Gaume and Alexander Puzrin, published a computer model showing how a small, delayed slab avalanche could have hit the tent hours after the hikers dug into the slope, causing injuries like the ones found. It's the best explanation we have. Critics still point out that the searchers saw no obvious avalanche debris, so the case isn't fully closed in everyone's mind.

known: Nine experienced hikers died after leaving their tent on the night of 1–2 February 1959.
The tent was cut open from the inside, and most of the group left without boots or warm outer clothing.

known.text: Footprints led about 1.5 km downhill toward the forest. Searchers found no sign of anyone else.

known: Six died of hypothermia. Three had severe skull or chest injuries caused by a strong force, not by a fight.
Some clothing showed traces of radioactivity.
The 1959 investigation blamed a "compelling natural force" and named no one.
In 2020 Russian prosecutors officially concluded that an avalanche and poor visibility were to blame.
A 2021 peer-reviewed study showed that a small, delayed slab avalanche on that slope was physically possible.
speculation: **Secret weapons test.** Some point to orange lights reported in the sky that winter. These are generally linked to Soviet missile launches on other dates, and no evidence ties a test to that night.
**Attack by local Mansi people.** Investigators looked into this early and dropped it. The footprints showed no one else, and nothing was taken from the tent.

speculation.text: **A yeti, or the Mansi "menk".** A favourite of documentaries. There's no physical evidence at all, and searchers found only the hikers' own footprints.

speculation: **A KGB plot.** One theory says some hikers were secret agents meeting spies. It's a fun thriller plot, but there are no documents or evidence behind it.
**Infrasound panic.** Wind around the mountain might create low-frequency sound that causes dread. It's an interesting idea that has never been tested at the site.

speculation.text: **Radiation means something sinister.** The traces were small and found on only some of the clothing. One hiker, Yuri Krivonishenko, is reported to have worked at a nuclear facility, which could explain contaminated clothing.

whyPeopleWonder: Dyatlov Pass has every ingredient that makes a mystery stick. The details are genuinely bizarre: a tent sliced open from the inside, people in socks in deadly cold, strange injuries. Each detail seems to demand its own explanation, and stacking them together feels like it must point to something huge.

Psychologists call this **proportionality bias**: we expect a big event to have a big cause. "A modest pile of snow slid onto a tent" feels too small to explain nine deaths, while a secret weapon or a monster feels the right size. On top of that, Soviet secrecy and a vague official verdict left a gap for decades, and gaps get filled with stories.
Finally, it feels personal. The hikers left diaries and photos, full of jokes and smiles, so they don't seem like names in a file. People want to give them a satisfying ending.
