stories.title: The Voynich *Manuscript*
stories.hook: A 600-year-old book written in an alphabet nobody can read, full of plants nobody can identify. Some of the world's best codebreakers have failed to crack it.
stories.verdictNote: Every announced "solution" so far has been rejected by experts.

story: In 1912 a rare-book dealer named Wilfrid Voynich bought a box of old manuscripts from a Jesuit college near Rome. One small book stood out. Its pages were covered in elegant handwriting in an alphabet no one had ever seen, alongside drawings of plants that botanists can't confidently identify, star charts, and little nude figures bathing in green pools connected by pipes.

Folded inside was a letter from 1665 or 1666 claiming that Emperor Rudolf II of Bohemia, a famous collector of strange things, had once paid 600 gold ducats for it. Voynich spent the rest of his life trying to find out what the book said. He never did.

Neither did anyone else. Over the following century the manuscript attracted professional codebreakers, including the American cryptographers who had broken enemy codes in two world wars. They failed. Linguists, historians, botanists and computer scientists have all had a go. Some announced breakthroughs, and every claim has fallen apart under expert review.

A few things we do know. In 2009 scientists radiocarbon-dated the vellum (the calfskin pages) to between **1404 and 1438**, so it's genuinely medieval, not a modern forgery. Statistical studies show the text has some patterns that look like real language, such as how often words repeat, but also strange features no known language has.

So is it a code, a lost language, an invented language, or a beautifully crafted hoax? Nobody knows. The manuscript now lives at Yale University, which has put every page online for free. Anyone can try to be the one who finally reads it.

known: The vellum has been radiocarbon-dated to 1404–1438. The ink was probably applied soon after, so the book isn't a modern forgery.
It has about 240 surviving pages. Some are fold-outs, and some pages are missing.
The script doesn't match any known writing system.
The text has some statistical patterns similar to natural languages, plus unusual repetitions that no known language shows.
It was bought by Wilfrid Voynich in 1912 and has been held by Yale University since 1969.
No proposed decipherment has been accepted by specialists.
speculation: **It's a cipher.** It would explain the strangeness, but no known cipher from the 1400s produces text that looks like this.
**It's a real language in a new alphabet.** Possible, perhaps a lost or poorly recorded language, but no candidate has convinced linguists.
**It's an elaborate hoax** made to impress or sell to collectors. Researchers have shown that gibberish with similar features *can* be produced, but whether it was is hotly debated.
**It's a women's health or herbal handbook.** A guess based on the bathing scenes and plant pictures. Without reading the text, it can't be tested.
**Roger Bacon wrote it.** Voynich's own favourite theory. The carbon dating rules it out: Bacon died in 1292.
whyPeopleWonder: The Voynich manuscript is a mystery you can hold. It's real, it's beautiful, and it's not hidden in a vault: Yale has put every page online. Anyone with a laptop can join the hunt, which makes it irresistible to amateurs and experts alike.

It also mixes two things our brains love: **patterns and gaps**. The text looks *almost* readable. Words repeat, sections have themes, and the pictures hint at meaning. That near-miss feeling keeps people sure they're just one insight away.
And it humbles us. In an age when computers can translate hundreds of languages, a little medieval book still refuses to talk.

funFact.text: Among the experts who failed to crack it was William Friedman, the codebreaker whose team broke Japan's top-secret "Purple" diplomatic cipher before Pearl Harbor. He suspected it was an early attempt at an invented, philosophical language.

stories.depthNote: Bottomless. Six centuries old, every page online, and a century of failed decipherments, rival theories and statistical studies.

stories.title: The Lost Colony of *Roanoke*
stories.hook: In 1587 about 115 English men, women and children settled on an island off North Carolina. Three years later their governor returned to find them gone, with a single word carved into a post.
stories.verdictNote: Most historians think the colonists split up and joined Native American communities, but no conclusive proof has been found.

story: In the 1580s, Sir Walter Raleigh set out to plant England's first permanent colony in North America. A first attempt on Roanoke Island, in what is now North Carolina, struggled: short of supplies and at odds with some of the local Native peoples, the settlers sailed home in 1586.

In 1587 Raleigh tried again. About 115 colonists, including families with children, sailed under a new governor, **John White**, an artist who had been on the earlier voyage. They were meant to settle on Chesapeake Bay, but their pilot, Simon Fernandes, refused to take them further and left them on Roanoke. On 18 August, White's daughter Eleanor gave birth to a girl, **Virginia Dare**: the first English child born in an English colony in the Americas.

White sailed back to England for supplies, planning to return in 1588. But England was at war with Spain, the Spanish Armada was coming, and every ship was needed at home. He didn't get back to Roanoke until 1590.

He found the settlement fortified but abandoned. The word **CROATOAN** was carved into a post of the palisade. Croatoan was the island home of the colony's Native ally, Manteo, and White took it to mean the colonists had moved there. Before he could follow the lead, rough seas and a lost anchor forced his ship back to England. He never saw his daughter or granddaughter again.

What happened has been argued over for more than 400 years. Most historians think the colonists split up and joined Native communities, and archaeologists have found European objects at Native sites on Hatteras Island and at a mainland site nicknamed "Site X". Tree rings show that 1587 to 1589 brought an extreme drought, a terrible time to start a colony. But no one has yet proven exactly where they went.

known: About 115 colonists arrived on Roanoke Island in 1587 under Governor John White.
Virginia Dare was born there on 18 August 1587.
War with Spain delayed White's return until 1590.
He found the settlement fortified but deserted, with "CROATOAN" carved on a post.
Croatoan Island was home to the people of Manteo, the colony's Native ally.
Tree-ring evidence shows an extreme drought in the region from 1587 to 1589.
speculation: **They joined the Croatoan people on Hatteras Island.** The most popular view. Archaeologists have found European artefacts, such as parts of a sword and a gun, at a Native village there, but dating and interpretation are debated.
**They moved inland to "Site X".** Tudor-era pottery has been found there, but it could also have come through trade.
**They were killed.** Jamestown colonists heard reports of a massacre, possibly by the Powhatan. No evidence has confirmed it.
**A Spanish attack.** Spanish records show Spain knew about Raleigh's plans, but there's no evidence of an attack on the colony.
**The Dare Stones tell their fate.** Inscribed stones found from 1937 to 1941 claimed to be messages from Eleanor Dare; most historians believe they're a fraud.
whyPeopleWonder: Roanoke has everything a mystery needs: a vanished community, a missing baby who became a national symbol, and one eerie word carved into wood.
It also sits at the very start of English America, so the story has been retold for centuries as a kind of origin myth, in books, in Paul Green's long-running play and in television horror.
And there's a real chance of an answer. Archaeology, tree rings, old maps and DNA research keep producing new clues, so each generation gets to hope it will be the one to solve it.

stories.title: The Loch Ness *Monster*
stories.hook: A long neck rising from a dark Scottish loch. Since 1933 thousands of people say they've seen her. The most famous photo turned out to be a toy. So what's really down there?
stories.verdictNote: No physical evidence has ever been found, and the most famous photo was a hoax. A 2018 DNA survey found no reptile DNA, but a surprising amount of eel DNA.

story: Loch Ness is a long, deep, peat-dark lake in the Scottish Highlands. It holds more fresh water than all the lakes in England and Wales combined. In 1933, the road along its shore had just been improved, and on 15 April a local couple, Aldie and John Mackay, reported seeing an enormous creature rolling in the water. On 2 May *The Inverness Courier* printed the story, describing a "beast" or "whale-like fish".

That July, George Spicer and his wife said they saw "a most extraordinary form of animal" cross the road in front of their car. Letters poured in, newspapers ran with it, and the Loch Ness monster was born. By the 1940s she had a nickname: **Nessie**.

In April 1934 came the most famous picture of all: the **"surgeon's photograph"**, credited to a respected London doctor and showing a small head on a long neck. For 60 years it was the best "evidence". By 1994 the truth was out: it was a toy submarine with a sculpted head, part of a revenge plot by the big-game hunter Marmaduke Wetherell, whom the *Daily Mail* had ridiculed over fake "Nessie footprints". His stepson, Christian Spurling, had built it.

Scientists have searched seriously. In 1987, Operation Deepscan sent a line of 24 boats with sonar sweeping across the loch. Others lowered cameras and robots. Sonar picked up a few contacts that were hard to explain, but nothing that proved a large animal. Many sightings turn out to be boat wakes on calm water, birds, otters, floating logs, or tricks of the light.

In 2018, scientists collected water samples from all over the loch and catalogued the DNA of everything living in it. They found no reptile DNA, no sturgeon, catfish or sharks, but a lot of eel DNA. The team's leader, Neil Gemmell, said they couldn't rule out unusually large eels, though none has ever been caught. Nessie remains unproven: no evidence of a monster, and a few eels to wonder about.

known: Loch Ness is the largest body of fresh water in the British Isles by volume, and about 230 m deep at its deepest.
The modern legend began in 1933, after the Mackays' reported sighting.
The 1934 "surgeon's photograph" was a hoax using a toy submarine.
Sonar sweeps such as Operation Deepscan (1987) found no conclusive evidence of a large animal.
A 2018 environmental-DNA survey found no reptile or large-fish DNA, but a lot of eel DNA.
The loch is only about 10,000 years old; before the end of the last Ice Age it was frozen.
speculation: **A surviving plesiosaur.** Plesiosaurs died out with the dinosaurs, the loch has existed only about 10,000 years, and experts say a plesiosaur couldn't lift its head swan-like out of the water. Air-breathing animals would also be seen surfacing constantly.
**A giant eel.** The DNA survey found plenty of eels, but no unusually large one has ever been caught.
**Misidentified animals.** Otters, birds and swimming animals have explained many sightings.
**Waves, wakes and logs.** Boat wakes can travel across calm water long after the boat has passed, looking like a moving hump.
**Deliberate hoaxes.** The surgeon's photograph, fake footprints and doctored photos show that some "evidence" was faked.
whyPeopleWonder: Loch Ness is genuinely mysterious to look at: deep, dark with peat and often misty. It's easy to imagine something hiding in it.

Wanting to believe plays a big part. A gentle monster is a fun idea, and every ripple becomes possible evidence. Psychologists call it **expectation bias**: when you're watching for Nessie, a log starts to look like a neck.
And Nessie is good for the Highlands. Visitors come from all over the world, and the legend is loved even by people who don't believe a word of it.
stories.funFact: In 2016 an underwater robot surveying Loch Ness found a monster on the bottom: a Nessie prop built for Billy Wilder's 1970 film *The Private Life of Sherlock Holmes*. The director had its humps removed, which ruined its buoyancy, and it sank during a test.

stories.title: Project *MKUltra*
stories.hook: For twenty years the CIA tested LSD, hypnosis and worse on people, many of whom never knew. It sounds like the wildest conspiracy theory. It's in the government's own records.
stories.verdictNote: Confirmed by the CIA's own surviving documents, a 1975 presidential commission and 1977 Senate hearings. What we'll never know is the full extent: most of the files were deliberately destroyed in 1973.

story: In April 1953, at the height of the Cold War, the director of the CIA approved a secret program with a strange name: **MKUltra**. Its goal was to find out whether the human mind could be controlled. Could a drug make a prisoner tell the truth? Could hypnosis make someone forget, or obey? The CIA feared that Soviet and Chinese interrogators had already discovered how to "brainwash" people, and it wanted to catch up.

The program was run by a CIA chemist named **Sidney Gottlieb**. Over the next decade it paid for 149 projects at more than 80 institutions, including universities, hospitals, prisons and drug companies, often hiding behind front organisations so the researchers didn't always know who was paying. Subjects were given LSD and other drugs, hypnotised, given electroshocks and deprived of sleep and sensation. Some were volunteers. Many were not. In San Francisco, in an operation called *Midnight Climax*, the CIA ran safehouses where men were secretly dosed with LSD and watched.

The human cost was real. In November 1953, an army scientist named **Frank Olson** was secretly given LSD by CIA colleagues at a retreat. Nine days later he fell to his death from a 13th-floor window of a New York hotel. In Montreal, the psychiatrist **Donald Ewen Cameron**, funded by MKUltra, put patients into drugged sleep for weeks while tape loops played the same messages over and over. Many were left with lasting damage.

In 1973, CIA director **Richard Helms** ordered the MKUltra files destroyed. It almost worked. But in 1975 a Senate committee led by Frank Church and a presidential commission revealed the program, and in 1977 a Freedom of Information Act request turned up about 20,000 documents that had survived because they'd been filed in the wrong building. They led to Senate hearings that same year.

So MKUltra is no theory. It's documented history, and it's also a warning. It found no reliable way to control anyone's mind, and Gottlieb came to believe it couldn't be done. But it showed that a government agency really did experiment on its own citizens in secret, which is one big reason people today find it easy to believe in other secret plots.

known: MKUltra was a real CIA program, approved on 13 April 1953 by Director Allen Dulles and run by Sidney Gottlieb.
Between 1953 and 1964 it funded 149 projects at more than 80 institutions, often through front organisations.
It used American and Canadian citizens as unwitting test subjects for LSD and other drugs, hypnosis, electroshock and sensory deprivation.
Frank Olson died in 1953, nine days after CIA colleagues secretly dosed him with LSD. His family received $750,000 and apologies from President Ford and CIA director William Colby.
Canada later settled with 127 of Cameron's former patients for $100,000 each.
Helms ordered the files destroyed in 1973. About 20,000 documents survived because they were misfiled, and were found in 1977.
speculation: **MKUltra created real brainwashed assassins.** The "Manchurian Candidate" idea is popular, and some historians think it was one of the goals. But there's no evidence the CIA ever achieved it, and its own chief concluded that mind control didn't work.

**Frank Olson was murdered.** His family believes so. A 1994 forensic team found a head injury that most of its members thought happened before the fall, but a 1996 review by Manhattan prosecutors found no case to bring. Disputed.
**The Unabomber was made by MKUltra.** As a Harvard student, Ted Kaczynski took part in a harsh psychology study led by Henry Murray. Some writers link it to MKUltra; that has never been established.
**Gangster Whitey Bulger was a test subject.** Bulger said he was given LSD in an Atlanta prison in 1957. It fits what we know of the era, but the details are his own account.
**It never stopped.** There's no evidence the program continued after the early 1970s, though because most records were destroyed, its full history can't be checked.
whyPeopleWonder: MKUltra is the case that conspiracy believers point to first, and it's easy to see why. It proves that a government agency really did run a secret program against its own people, really did destroy the evidence, and really did get caught only by chance.
The missing files leave holes. When most of the records have been shredded, nobody can say for sure who else was tested, or what else was tried, and imaginations fill the gaps.

And the story reaches into pop culture: historian Stephen Kinzer argues that CIA-funded research helped spread LSD into the 1960s counterculture, and novelist Ken Kesey first took it as a paid volunteer.
stories.funFact: The 20,000 MKUltra documents that survived Richard Helms's order to destroy everything did so by accident: they had been stored in a financial records building instead of with the rest of the files.
stories.depthNote: Bottomless. Thousands of pages, hundreds of subprojects, missing files and decades of lawsuits.

stories.title: Operation *Northwoods*
stories.hook: In 1962 America's top generals signed a plan to stage fake terror attacks and blame them on Cuba, to start a war. The President said no. The world found out 35 years later.
stories.verdictNote: The plan is real: the declassified memo, signed by the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, is public. But it was rejected, and none of it was ever carried out.

story: In 1962 the United States badly wanted rid of Fidel Castro. The communist leader had taken power in Cuba, just off the coast of Florida, and a CIA-backed invasion at the Bay of Pigs had failed embarrassingly the year before. A secret campaign called Operation Mongoose was looking for any way to bring him down, and its chief, Brigadier General **Edward Lansdale**, asked the military for ideas.

The Joint Chiefs of Staff answered on 13 March 1962 with a top-secret memo: *"Justification for US Military Intervention in Cuba"*. Signed by their chairman, General **Lyman Lemnitzer**, it proposed creating fake reasons for war. Ideas included staging attacks on the US base at Guantanamo Bay, sinking boats of Cuban refugees, hijacking planes, a campaign of terror in Miami and Washington, and faking the shooting down of a civilian airliner. "We could blow up a U.S. ship in Guantanamo Bay and blame Cuba," it suggested.

It was a false flag plan: make the attacks look Cuban, so the American public and the world would back an invasion. The memo was delivered to the Secretary of Defense, **Robert McNamara**. Three days later, according to notes of a meeting, President **John F. Kennedy** told Lemnitzer bluntly that the US was not discussing the use of military force. Within months Lemnitzer was denied another term as chairman and moved to a post in Europe.

Northwoods wasn't the only idea. Another plan, *Operation Dirty Trick*, proposed blaming Cuba if astronaut John Glenn's space flight failed, by faking evidence of Cuban radio interference. Even in 1963 the Pentagon was still discussing a staged "Cuban" attack on a Caribbean neighbour such as Jamaica.

The memo stayed secret until 18 November 1997, when a board set up to release records on Kennedy's assassination made it public. It became famous in 2001 through James Bamford's book *Body of Secrets*. It's the clearest proof that senior officials really have proposed staging attacks on their own side, and also proof that, this time, the answer was no.

known: On 13 March 1962 the Joint Chiefs of Staff sent the Secretary of Defense a top-secret plan to create pretexts for invading Cuba.
It was signed by their chairman, General Lyman Lemnitzer, in response to a request from Operation Mongoose chief Edward Lansdale.
Its proposals included staged attacks on Guantanamo, sinking boats of Cuban refugees, hijackings, terror in US cities and a faked airliner shootdown.
Kennedy rejected military action, and none of the proposals was ever carried out.
Lemnitzer was denied a second term as chairman and moved to NATO in January 1963.
The memo was declassified on 18 November 1997 and published online by the National Security Archive in 2001.
speculation: **Northwoods proves 9/11 was an inside job.** It's often quoted this way. But Northwoods was rejected and never carried out, and a 1962 plan says nothing about who attacked in 2001. See our 9/11 file for the evidence.
**Kennedy was killed because he said no.** The military's anger at Kennedy over Cuba is well documented, but there's no evidence linking Northwoods to his assassination.
**Parts of it were secretly carried out.** None of the specific provocations in the memo ever happened.
**McNamara approved it.** It's unclear how he reacted. Either way, it wasn't implemented.
whyPeopleWonder: Northwoods is the document every false-flag theory reaches for. If the top generals of the United States could sign their names to a plan like this, the argument goes, what else might they have done?
That's a fair question, and it's why it matters that the plan is public. It shows exactly how such an idea was proposed, and also how it was stopped: by a civilian president who refused it.

And there's a twist that keeps it in the news: the memo only came out because of a law to release records about Kennedy's assassination, which links it forever to the most debated case in American history.
stories.funFact: One related idea, Operation Dirty Trick, planned to blame Cuba if John Glenn's 1962 space flight failed, by "manufacturing various pieces of evidence" of Cuban radio interference. Glenn orbited the Earth three times and came home safely.
stories.depthNote: Deep. A short memo, but it connects to Cuba, Kennedy, the Cold War and nearly every modern false-flag theory.

stories.title: The *Tunguska* Event
stories.hook: One summer morning in 1908, something exploded over Siberia with the force of a huge nuclear bomb and flattened 2,000 square kilometres of forest. It left no crater.
stories.verdictNote: The explosion is real and well documented, and scientists agree it was a space rock bursting in the air. What exactly it was, a stony asteroid or an icy comet, is still debated.

story: At about a quarter past seven on the morning of 30 June 1908, a fireball crossed the sky over central Siberia. At a trading post 60 kilometres away, a farmer named **Semyon Semyonov** said the sky "was split in two" and the whole northern sky seemed to be on fire. He felt heat as if his shirt were burning. Then came a bang, and the shock wave threw him off his porch.

Something had exploded several kilometres above the forest near the Podkamennaya Tunguska River. The blast flattened around **2,150 square kilometres** of trees, an area bigger than greater London, in a giant radial pattern. Windows shattered up to 200 kilometres away. Seismographs as far away as Germany recorded it, and for several nights the sky over Europe glowed so brightly that people could read outside at midnight.

The region was remote and Russia was soon caught up in war and revolution, so no scientists went for years. In 1927 the mineralogist **Leonid Kulik** finally reached the centre, guided by local Evenki hunters, expecting to find a giant crater and a meteorite worth mining. There was no crater. At the very centre, trees were still standing, stripped of their branches, while all around them millions more lay pointing outwards.

That was the clue. Scientists now agree that a rock from space, probably 50 to 60 metres across, exploded in the air 5 to 10 kilometres up, releasing energy usually estimated at **10 to 15 megatons**, around a thousand times the first atomic bomb test. Because it burst in the air, there was no impact crater, and no fragment of it has ever been firmly identified. In 2013 a much smaller airburst over Chelyabinsk, Russia, caught on hundreds of dashcams, showed how it happens.

Remarkably, the area was so empty that only a handful of people died: at least three Evenki herders. If the same object had exploded over a city, it could have destroyed it. Tunguska is now the benchmark for planetary defence, the science of spotting dangerous asteroids before they hit, and the United Nations marks its anniversary every year as International Asteroid Day.

known: On the morning of 30 June 1908 a huge explosion occurred in the air over central Siberia, near the Podkamennaya Tunguska River.
It flattened about 2,150 km² of forest in a radial pattern and broke windows up to 200 km away.
It killed at least three people, as well as many reindeer and other animals.
There is no impact crater. Scientists agree it was the airburst of an object from space.
Energy estimates range from 3 to 30 megatons; 10 to 15 is most often quoted.
No fragment has been formally identified, so whether it was an asteroid or a comet is still debated.
speculation: **It was a comet, not an asteroid.** A genuine scientific debate. Many researchers favour a stony asteroid, partly from how deep such objects get into the atmosphere, but it isn't settled.
**Lake Cheko is a crater from a fragment.** This small lake 8 km from the epicentre may not appear on records before 1908. Some studies support the idea; others say its sediments are much older.

**Nikola Tesla's "death ray" did it.** A popular legend. Tesla couldn't have known about the event until stories reached the American press in 1928, and the records of the Arctic expedition he supposedly used as a spotter show no contact with him.
**It was an alien spaceship or a tiny black hole.** Great science fiction. No evidence supports either.
**It knocked down 80 million trees.** An often-quoted number, but researchers have traced it to a loose 1934 estimate. It's an overestimate.
whyPeopleWonder: Tunguska is the biggest impact event in recorded history, and it left no crater and no meteorite. A missing "murder weapon" is irresistible.

It's also a reminder that space can still surprise us. Estimates suggest a Tunguska-sized airburst happens somewhere on Earth every 300 to 1,000 years, and most of Earth is ocean or wilderness, so a lot of what happens goes unwitnessed.
And it shows how mysteries get solved. The answer came not from one discovery but from Evenki testimony, fallen trees, seismographs, physics, and finally the cameras that filmed Chelyabinsk.
stories.funFact: Because of Tunguska, 30 June is International Asteroid Day, declared by the United Nations in 2016 to raise awareness of planetary defence.
stories.depthNote: Moderate. The science is clear on the basics, but comet-versus-asteroid and Lake Cheko keep researchers busy.

stories.title: The Dancing Plague of *1518*
stories.hook: One July day in Strasbourg, a woman started dancing in the street and couldn't stop. Within weeks, dozens or even hundreds of people were dancing with her, for days on end.
stories.verdictNote: The outbreak is recorded by physicians, preachers, chroniclers and the city council. Why it happened, and whether anyone actually danced to death, is still debated.

story: In the middle of July 1518, a woman in Strasbourg stepped out into the narrow street outside her home and began to dance. There was no music and no celebration. She simply kept going, hour after hour, day after day, stopping only to sleep. Most of the chronicles that record it call her **Frau Troffea**.

Then others joined in. Within days more than thirty people were dancing. By August, chroniclers counted somewhere between 50 and 400. They weren't enjoying themselves: witnesses described thrashing arms, vacant eyes, swollen and bleeding feet, and cries for help. People collapsed from exhaustion.

The city's leaders consulted the physicians, who blamed "overheated blood" and prescribed an unusual cure: **more dancing**. The council opened guild halls and hired musicians and strong men to keep the dancers moving. It made things worse. So the council changed its mind, banned public dancing and music, and sent the afflicted to a shrine of Saint Vitus, the saint believed to curse sinners with dancing. They were given red shoes marked with crosses and prayed for forgiveness. By early September, the outbreak faded away.

We know this happened because it's recorded in physicians' notes, cathedral sermons, local and regional chronicles, and the city council's own records. What we don't know is *why*. Some have blamed ergot, a fungus on rye bread that contains a chemical related to LSD. The historian **John Waller** argues instead for a mass psychogenic illness: a population worn down by famine, disease and fear of Saint Vitus's curse, falling into a kind of collective trance.

And did people really dance to death? Some modern retellings say as many as fifteen a day died. But the Strasbourg records written at the time don't mention any deaths at all; those claims come from later accounts. Strasbourg wasn't unique either. Outbreaks of "dancing mania" were reported along the Rhine and Moselle rivers from the 14th century onwards, but 1518 is the best documented of them all.

known: In July 1518, a woman began dancing uncontrollably in a Strasbourg street. Four of the six chronicle accounts name her as Frau Troffea.
Over the summer, somewhere between 50 and 400 people were affected.
It's documented in physicians' notes, cathedral sermons, chronicles and city council records.
The council first encouraged the dancing with halls and musicians, then banned public dancing and music.
Dancers were taken to a shrine of Saint Vitus, and the outbreak ended in early September.
Similar "dancing mania" outbreaks were recorded in the region from the 14th to the 17th centuries.
speculation: **Dozens or hundreds danced to death.** Often repeated, sometimes as "fifteen a day". But the city's records from the time don't mention deaths; the claims come from later accounts. Unknown.

**Ergot poisoning.** A fungus on rye, related to LSD. Waller argues that people poisoned by ergot couldn't have danced for days, that so many wouldn't react the same way, and that it can't explain why outbreaks clustered along the Rhine and Moselle rivers.
**Mass psychogenic illness.** The most popular explanation: extreme stress from famine and disease, plus belief in Saint Vitus's curse. It fits the evidence, but can't be proven 500 years later.
**Exact numbers.** Estimates range from 50 to 400 dancers. The sources simply don't agree.
whyPeopleWonder: It sounds like a folk tale, but it's in the city's own records. That gap, between how impossible it sounds and how well it's documented, is what makes it so gripping.
It's also a story about the human mind. Mass psychogenic illness still happens today, in schools and workplaces, and 1518 is one of its most dramatic examples.
And it keeps returning in art: short films, novels and pop songs have all taken their beat from Strasbourg's dancers.
stories.funFact: Strasbourg's first official cure was more dancing. The council opened guild halls and hired musicians so the dancers could "dance themselves free" of it. When that backfired, it banned music in public instead.
stories.depthNote: Moderate. Rich sources from the time, but the cause and the death toll are still argued over.

stories.title: The Great *Emu* War
stories.hook: In 1932 the Australian Army sent soldiers with machine guns to fight 20,000 emus. The emus did not lose.
stories.verdictNote: It really happened, and it's well documented in newspapers, parliament and army reports. Only the "war" part is a joke: it was a military cull, and how many birds were killed is disputed.

story: After World War I, Australia gave thousands of returning soldiers land to farm in Western Australia, much of it marginal country on the edge of the wheatbelt. Then the Great Depression hit. Wheat prices fell, promised government help never came, and in 1932 the farmers faced a new enemy: about **20,000 emus**.

Emus migrate towards the coast after breeding, and they found the farms ideal, with cleared land, water troughs and fields of wheat. They ate and trampled the crops and broke the fences, letting rabbits in. So a group of ex-soldier farmers went to the Defence Minister, **Sir George Pearce**, with a request they knew from the trenches: send machine guns.

Pearce agreed. In November 1932, **Major G. P. W. Meredith** of the Royal Australian Artillery arrived in the Campion district with two soldiers, two Lewis guns and 10,000 rounds of ammunition. It went badly. The emus scattered into small groups and ran out of range. At an ambush by a dam, a thousand birds approached, but the gun jammed after twelve were killed. A gun mounted on a truck couldn't keep up, and the ride was too bumpy to shoot. The newspapers had a field day, and they called it the **Emu War**.

After a week of ridicule, the soldiers were withdrawn on 8 November. But the farmers kept asking for help, the Premier of Western Australia backed them, and Meredith was sent back. By 10 December he reported 986 confirmed kills for 9,860 rounds, exactly ten bullets per bird, and claimed 2,500 more had died of wounds. Historians think those figures are probably inflated. The crops were still being eaten.

When farmers asked for the army again in 1934, 1943 and 1948, the government refused. Bounties for hunters and long emu-proof fences did far more. The emus are still there. Today they appear on Australia's coat of arms, and the Emu War lives on as one of the internet's favourite true stories.

known: In late 1932, about 20,000 emus moved onto farmland in the Campion district of Western Australia.
Ex-soldier farmers asked Defence Minister Sir George Pearce for machine guns, and he agreed.
Major G. P. W. Meredith led two soldiers with two Lewis guns and 10,000 rounds of ammunition.
The first attempt (2 to 8 November) was withdrawn after poor results and public ridicule.
In the second (13 November to 10 December), Meredith claimed 986 kills with 9,860 rounds.
Later requests for military help were refused; bounties and exclusion fences were used instead.
speculation: **Australia declared war on emus.** No. It was a military-assisted cull. The newspapers named it the Emu War.
**The emus won.** In a sense. The army failed to solve the problem and withdrew, but it did kill hundreds of birds, and one newspaper in 1935 claimed it saved the wheat.

**The emus had generals.** Army observers said each group had a tall black-plumed leader keeping watch, and ornithologist Dominic Serventy joked that the "Emu command" had ordered guerrilla tactics. Emus naturally scatter when threatened.
**Meredith's numbers.** 986 kills plus 2,500 wounded birds dying later is the official claim. Historians call it highly disputed and probably inflated.
whyPeopleWonder: It's genuinely funny: a modern army, machine guns, and a flightless bird that wins on points. The internet discovered it decades later and turned it into a legend.
But it's also a real story about hard times. The farmers were veterans, ruined by the Depression, facing a disaster in their fields with little help from their government.
And it carries a serious lesson about wildlife: firepower doesn't fix an ecological problem. Fences and better land management did more than any machine gun.
stories.funFact: According to one newspaper report, the soldiers were also told to collect 100 emu skins, so that the feathers could decorate the slouch hats of Australia's Light Horse regiments.
stories.depthNote: Shallow but delightful. Easy to read, hard to forget.
